主要内容: On November 1, 2017, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) published Staff Legal Bulletin No. 14I (CF), providing guidance on Rule 14a-8 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. This bulletin outlines the Division of Corporation Finance’s views on the scope and application of Rule 14a-8(i)(7), which allows companies to exclude shareholder proposals related to ordinary business operations. The purpose of the exception is to ensure that management and the board of directors handle day-to-day business decisions, as it is impractical for shareholders to address such matters at annual meetings. The Division emphasizes that proposals focusing on significant policy issues that transcend ordinary business may still be appropriate for shareholder votes. Companies seeking no-action relief under Rule 14a-8(i)(7) are expected to provide detailed board analysis of the policy issue and its significance, ensuring well-informed and reasoned decisions. The SEC's Staff Legal Bulletin No. 14I (CF) also outlines the application of Rule 14a-8(i)(5), which allows companies to exclude shareholder proposals that are not economically relevant. The rule permits exclusion if the proposal relates to operations accounting for less than 5% of total assets, net earnings, and gross sales, and is not significantly related to the company’s business. The SEC has historically interpreted this rule narrowly, focusing on whether the company conducted any business related to the issue, rather than the proposal’s significance to the company’s operations. The Division’s approach has been criticized for unduly limiting the exclusion’s availability by not fully considering the second prong of the rule, which assesses whether the proposal deals with a matter not significantly related to the issuer’s business. Going forward, the Division will focus on the proposal’s significance to the company’s business when it relates to operations accounting for less than 5% of total assets, net earnings, and gross sales. This shift aims to align the application of the rule with its intended purpose. The SEC's Staff Legal Bulletin No. 14I (CF) outlines the criteria for determining whether a shareholder proposal is 'otherwise significantly related to the company’s business' under Rule 14a-8(i)(5). The analysis depends on the specific circumstances of the company, as a matter significant to one company may not be significant to another. Substantive governance matters are generally considered significantly related to most companies. If a proposal's significance is not apparent, the proponent must demonstrate that it is 'otherwise significantly related to the company’s business.' This can include showing potential impacts on other business segments or significant contingent liabilities. The staff will evaluate proposals in light of the 'total mix' of information about the issuer. The board of directors is better positioned to assess the significance of a proposal due to their knowledge of the company's business. The Division will no longer rely on the analysis under Rule 14a-8(i)(7) when evaluating Rule 14a-8(i)(5) proposals, as separate frameworks will better serve the intended purpose of each exclusion basis. The SEC has issued guidance on shareholder proposals under Rule 14a-8, emphasizing the need for clear documentation when submitting proposals by proxy. The guidance outlines that proposals must include specific details such as the shareholder-proponent, the company involved, the meeting for which the proposal is submitted, and the specific proposal content. This documentation is intended to help alleviate concerns about proxy-based proposals and assist companies in evaluating whether the eligibility requirements of Rule 14a-8(b) have been met. If this information is not provided, there may be a basis to exclude the proposal under Rule 14a-8(b). Additionally, the SEC has clarified that the use of graphs and images in shareholder proposals is permissible under Rule 14a-8(d), as long as they do not make the proposal materially false, misleading, or irrelevant. The SEC also notes that the total word count, including words in graphics, must not exceed 500 words. These guidelines aim to ensure transparency and clarity in shareholder proposals while allowing for the use of visual aids to convey information effectively.
